title: 0. Long-term SDK shape: do we want an SDK at all in the current form?
description:
Strategic question lifted verbatim from the AALGO-216 notes doc: 'Do we see us having an SDK in the same way we currently do long term?'

This is a chunk-0 (gate) decision — if the answer changes the SDK's shape (or kills the SDK as a separate artifact), it reframes every chunk below it. Resolve before pouring time into chunks 4-8.

Today's shape:
- Python SDK generated by Stainless, lives in a separate Git repo, vendored back into this monorepo (nemo-platform-sdk package).
- Studio web SDK generated separately (update-web-sdk).
- CLI in packages/nemo_platform_ext/.../cli is the primary in-repo consumer of the Python SDK.
- External: published-but-not-on-PyPI; partners/customers don't broadly consume it today.

Alternative shapes to consider:
- Keep the Python SDK + TS web SDK split (status quo, just a new generator).
- Collapse: ship only a CLI; the CLI talks to the API via a thin generated client embedded in the CLI package, no externally-distributed SDK.
- MCP-first: the primary 'SDK' is an MCP server, with code SDKs as a secondary derivative.
- Typed-RPC (gRPC, Connect, tRPC-style): regenerate clients from a typed RPC schema instead of OpenAPI; SDK becomes a thin protobuf or schema-derived client.
- Hybrid: keep a Python SDK for internal/CLI use, but de-prioritize external SDK distribution.

Questions:
- Who actually depends on an external NeMo SDK today? Who is forecasted to in 12 months?
- Is the CLI (or an MCP server) sufficient as the public interface for most users?
- If we keep the SDK shape, are we honest that the CLI is the primary consumer and shape the SDK for that?
- What does the Studio web team need from the TS SDK that a generated OpenAPI client wouldn't give?

Deliverable: a one-page decision on long-term SDK shape, attached to this issue. Hands the answer off to chunk 3 (multi-language scope), chunk 4 (generator survey), chunk 5 (distribution strategy), and chunk 6 (spike). All four will narrow their scope based on this.

Complexity: low-med (it's a strategic decision, not a build). Impact: highest — wrong answer here makes the rest of the investigation answer the wrong question.

title: 1. Audit current Stainless pain & OpenAPI workarounds
description:
Catalog every workaround we currently absorb so the rest of the investigation has a concrete defect list to score against.

Inputs to read:
- script/generate_openapi_spec.py — list each post-processing pass (rename_schema_references, reorder_spec, hoist_nested_defs, fix_recursive_schemas, fix_ref_with_additional_props, remove_endpoint, fix_openai_streaming_endpoints, remove_unused_schemas, remove_invalid_components, etc.) with file:line and the OpenAPI/Stainless quirk each one papers over.
- script/openapi_helper/ — supporting transforms.
- sdk/stainless.yaml — custom_casings, query_settings, edition pinning, edition workarounds (e.g. python_version_range comment about .python-version 3.9.18), targets/options.
- CLI usage of the generated SDK in packages/nemo_platform_ext/src/nemo_platform_ext/cli — note any places the CLI has to wrap, retype, or work around generated code.
- Studio web SDK consumers via update-web-sdk.
- Recent commits / PRs touching openapi or sdk for additional pain points.

Deliverable: a short defects-we-absorb document inside this issue (bd note --append-notes) covering: (a) workarounds we'd inherit if we kept any OpenAPI-based generator, (b) workarounds specific to Stainless's behavior, (c) consumer pain (typed-wrong, missing async, missing retries, etc.).

Complexity: low. Impact: high — every later chunk references this list.

title: 2. Define the SDK target rubric
description:
Write the rubric we will score every candidate against. Stainless's own pitch (consistency/compatibility/distribution) and Speakeasy's Python comparison page (https://www.speakeasy.com/docs/sdks/languages/python/oss-comparison-python) seed the menu; the audit in chunk 1 supplies the must-haves.

Dimensions to grade (each must-have / nice-to-have / out-of-scope):
- Type fidelity: Pydantic v2 models, TypedDict alongside, discriminated unions, optional-vs-nullable, generics, enums (native Enum vs string-validated), open enums.
- Async: native async client via httpx; sync wrapper.
- Resilience: retries with backoff, configurable per-operation; pagination helpers; timeouts.
- Protocols: SSE / streaming, file uploads (multipart), websockets if relevant.
- Auth: bearer, OAuth, OpenID, custom header schemes.
- Servers: multiple servers / environments; per-call base URL override.
- Errors: typed exception hierarchy, response envelope handling, request-id propagation.
- Ergonomics: idiomatic naming, snake_case, casing overrides (cf. NeMo/NER/PII/LLM in stainless.yaml), zero-config sensible defaults.
- Observability: hooks for logging, OTEL, request/response interception.
- Ancillary: MCP server target, mock server, code samples in docs, changelog gen.
- Engineering: source-of-truth model, drift detection, generated-code review burden, CI integration.

Deliverable: rubric document attached to this issue (bd note --append-notes) with each dimension marked must/nice/out and a short justification.

Complexity: low-med. Impact: high — defines what 'good' means.
notes: Canonical framing from the doc: 'What do we need from an SDK?' This rubric is the answer. Speakeasy's comparison page (https://www.speakeasy.com/docs/sdks/languages/python/oss-comparison-python) seeds the menu; pair with Fern's quickstart for cross-check (https://buildwithfern.com/learn/sdks/generators/python/quickstart).

title: 3. Multi-language scope decision
description:
Decide which target languages we must support; this gates every later chunk. Today Stainless is configured Python-only (TS target commented out in sdk/stainless.yaml). Studio web has its own update-web-sdk path. Stainless supports Python/TS/Go/Java/Kotlin if we ever re-enable them.

Questions to answer:
- Who consumes the SDK today? (Our CLI = Python; Studio web = TS via web-sdk; external partners = ?)
- Is there a roadmap commitment to TS/Go/etc. SDKs for external customers?
- If Python-only is acceptable, build-yourself becomes dramatically cheaper (one target, one code-generator, no cross-language discipline). If multi-target is required, that pushes us toward Stainless/Speakeasy/Fern rather than custom.
- What is the bar for TS? Is the existing update-web-sdk output good enough, or do we want a real first-class TS SDK?

Deliverable: a one-page decision recording target list, owner, and consequences, attached to this issue.

Complexity: low (it's a decision, not a build). Impact: high — scopes chunks 4-7.

title: Stainless replacement investigation
description:
Umbrella for the investigation tracked in the Linear notes doc. The driving question is: do we keep paying Stainless, switch to another SDK generator (Speakeasy/Fern/etc.), or build something ourselves — possibly skipping OpenAPI entirely by generating clients straight from FastAPI route definitions.

Today the SDK pipeline is: FastAPI routes -> script/generate_openapi_spec.py (~15 post-processing passes) -> openapi/openapi.yaml -> Stainless (sdk/stainless.yaml, Python-only; TS + MCP targets commented out) -> vendored back, consumed by the CLI in packages/nemo_platform_ext/.../cli and by Studio web via update-web-sdk.

Children below break the question into chunks to tackle in dedicated sessions. Order encodes tackle sequence (1 first).
notes:
Forced-migration context (from AALGO-216 notes doc, 2026-05-21):
- Stainless is going 'source available' to existing users but will NOT maintain it, and we cannot distribute it. So we cannot use it even in the near term.
- Three options Max already framed in the doc:
  1) Existing OAPIG generator (Max used at Gretel, 'had to hack some internals to get good bindings').
  2) New provider — Speakeasy or Fern — accept another lock-in.
  3) Roll our own (scripts + agents).
- Pre-RFC questions still open:
  - How do we feel about getting pulled into yet another cloud platform for generating SDKs?
  - Do we see us having an SDK in the same way we currently do long term?
  - Can we vibe a better OAPIG plugin?
  - What do we need from an SDK?

title: 8. Synthesis: build / buy / hybrid decision + Stainless exit ramp
description:
Compose findings from chunks 1-7 into the actual decision. This is the final deliverable of the investigation.

Required content:
- Recommendation: stay on Stainless / switch to Speakeasy or Fern / hybrid (e.g. Stainless for TS, custom for Python) / full custom from FastAPI source.
- Feature-parity matrix using the chunk-2 rubric, scoring every option.
- Cost-to-build estimate (eng-weeks) for any non-stay option.
- Cost-to-maintain estimate (annual hours).
- Risk register: CVE exposure, generated-code drift, breaking changes from upstream, multi-language gap if we go Python-only, lock-in concerns.
- Exit ramp from Stainless: how does already-generated code migrate? (Stainless output is in a separate repo; do we cut over with a flag day, or run parallel?)
- A go/no-go gate.

This issue depends on 1-7 finishing first.

Complexity: high. Impact: highest — this is the actual answer to the driving question.
notes:
Per the doc this is the RFC deliverable for AALGO-216 — should produce a concrete migration recommendation, not just findings. Time pressure: Stainless is going source-available + we cannot distribute it, so we have to land on a path before that bites. Synthesis should pick exactly one of:
- Switch to Fern (commercial, multi-target).
- Switch to Speakeasy (commercial, multi-target).
- Fork/extend OAPIG with a NeMo plugin (branch A of the spike).
- Skip OpenAPI: from-source codegen (branch B of the spike).
- Hybrid (e.g. fork OAPIG for TS, from-source for Python).
Each option needs cost-to-build, cost-to-maintain, lock-in posture, multi-language coverage, exit ramp.

title: 4. Survey OSS / commercial SDK generators against the rubric
description:
Apply the chunk-2 rubric to every credible alternative; pick 1-2 finalists for a hands-on trial against openapi/openapi.yaml. If something off-the-shelf wins outright, the investigation can end here.

Candidates to score:
- Speakeasy (commercial; per their comparison page, has TypedDict + Pydantic, native enums, async via httpx, retries, pagination, OAuth, open enums via x-speakeasy-unknown-values, multi-server).
- Fern (commercial with OSS generators; multi-target).
- openapi-python-client (Heynes, OSS, Python-only).
- OpenAPI Generator (OSS, multi-target, known to produce un-idiomatic Python — see speakeasy comparison).
- hey-api (OSS, TS-focused but worth checking Python story).
- Kiota (Microsoft, multi-target, opinionated client model).
- datamodel-code-generator + a hand-rolled client layer (lowest-rung hybrid).

For each: license, languages, type fidelity, async, retries, pagination, streaming, OAuth, multi-server, extensibility, drift handling, community/maintenance signal.

Hands-on trial: run the top two against openapi/openapi.yaml, generate a small slice, inspect a couple of representative operations (e.g. an LLM-as-judge eval and a model invoke) and compare to today's Stainless output.

Deliverable: matrix + finalist recommendation in this issue.

Complexity: med. Impact: high — may shortcut chunks 6 and 8.
notes:
Per the doc:
- Max's OAPIG experience at Gretel: needed to hack internals for usable bindings — factor that into the OAPIG row of the matrix.
- Lock-in concern is named explicitly: 'How do we feel about getting pulled into yet another cloud platform for generating SDKs?' Weight Fern/Speakeasy on portability of generated output and ease of exiting their pipeline if they pull a Stainless on us.

title: 5. Distribution, versioning, and release strategy
description:
If we leave Stainless, we own packaging+distribution. Decide what that looks like before we build it. This chunk is orthogonal to the codegen mechanism — same answer needed whether we switch vendors or build custom.

Today's flow (per AGENTS.md SDK Generation section):
- Generated SDK lives in a separate Git repo, vendored back into this monorepo via make stainless.
- Versioning is Stainless edition-pinned (python.2025-11-20 in sdk/stainless.yaml).
- PyPI publish is disabled (publish.pypi: false).

Questions to answer:
- Source-of-truth location: keep the generated SDK in its own repo, move it into this monorepo, or publish-only?
- Versioning model: date-based (per Stainless), semver, or follow platform API version?
- PyPI: do we publish externally? Pre-release / nightly channel? Internal index only?
- Vendoring back: is the monorepo vendor pattern keeping us safer, or is it just inertia?
- Changelog: hand-rolled vs auto-generated from OpenAPI diffs.
- Update cadence: gated on every PR that touches an API file, or scheduled?
- Studio web SDK (update-web-sdk) — separate or unified?

Deliverable: a release-strategy document attached to this issue.

Complexity: med. Impact: med — required regardless of codegen choice.

title: 6. Spike: skip-OpenAPI codegen from FastAPI source
description:
The 'musings of a madman' chunk: prototype a generator that introspects FastAPI routes and Pydantic models directly and emits a typed Python client (and a typer CLI) without going through OpenAPI as an intermediate. We own both ends; we may not need the lossy intermediate.

The thesis to test: most of the ~15 post-processing passes in script/generate_openapi_spec.py exist because OpenAPI 3.x cannot faithfully express what Pydantic v2 already expresses (recursive refs, discriminated unions, additionalProperties with refs, generics, streaming endpoints, etc.). Going Pydantic-to-client direct should eliminate that whole class of workaround and yield better type fidelity than any OpenAPI-based generator can.

Scope (intentionally narrow):
- Pick ONE service or API slice (suggest: namespaces or models — pick a small one with non-trivial types).
- Walk FastAPI route table; for each route, extract path, method, request model, response model, status codes, deprecations.
- Resolve Pydantic types into a typed client method (sync + async).
- Generate matching typer CLI commands.
- Don't try to handle every edge case; document what falls off the table.

Measurements:
- Generator LOC.
- Lines of post-processing eliminated vs script/generate_openapi_spec.py.
- Type fidelity for the slice (discriminated unions, recursive refs, generics, streaming).
- Multi-language story (does this approach extend to TS at all, or is it Python-only by construction?).

Deliverable: a runnable spike branch + a writeup attached here. Result is binary: this either feels obviously better than Stainless output or it doesn't. Either result kills or confirms the hypothesis.

Complexity: high. Impact: high — proves or kills the user's hypothesis.
notes:
Per the doc, this chunk now covers TWO branches of 'option 3 — roll our own', evaluated side-by-side:

Branch A — 'Can we vibe a better OAPIG plugin?' (incremental)
- Fork or extend openapi-python-client / OpenAPI Generator with a custom template + Python post-processor.
- Re-uses the existing openapi/openapi.yaml; lets us keep that intermediate and the script/generate_openapi_spec.py infra (mostly).
- Lower risk, lower ceiling — still bound by OpenAPI 3.x expressiveness limits.
- Cheaper to maintain because we only own the template/plugin, not a whole generator.

Branch B — Skip OpenAPI entirely, generate from FastAPI source (radical)
- Walk FastAPI route table + resolve Pydantic models directly into client + CLI.
- Eliminates the ~15-pass post-processor pipeline in script/generate_openapi_spec.py because Pydantic doesn't have OpenAPI's expressiveness gaps (recursive refs, ref-with-additionalProps, discriminated unions, generics, streaming).
- Higher ceiling on type fidelity (the user's hypothesis), higher cost, Python-only by construction.
- Multi-language story is harder — we lose OpenAPI as the polyglot serialization point.

The spike should produce both prototypes against the same small slice (e.g. namespaces or models) and score them on: lines of generator/template code, type fidelity, eliminated workarounds, multi-language extensibility, expected maintenance cost. Result feeds chunk 8 (synthesis).

title: 7. MCP server generation strategy
description:
Stainless's typescript target in sdk/stainless.yaml has a commented-out MCP server option (enable_all_resources: true). Decide whether we want first-party MCP exposure of the NeMo API and, if so, whether we can generate it cleanly from the same source as chunk 6.

Questions:
- Is there real demand for an MCP server in front of NeMo (agents talking to NeMo via MCP)? Who would consume it?
- If we keep Stainless, can we just flip the TS target back on and get the MCP server for free? What's the output quality?
- If we move off Stainless, does the chunk-6 from-source path generate MCP tool definitions as cheaply as it generates Python clients? (FastAPI routes -> MCP tools is a small mapping.)
- Auth / security model for an MCP front of the API.

Deliverable: a recommendation on whether MCP is in scope at all, and if so the generation path.

Complexity: med. Impact: med-low — depends on MCP demand.
